chain.g: amorous play, piece of fun or entertainment

ety.text: Inherited from Middle English toye (“amorous play, piece of fun or entertainment”), probably from Middle Dutch toy, tuyg (“tools, apparatus, utensil, ornament”) as in Dutch speel-tuig (“plaything, toy”), from Old Dutch *tiug, from Proto-West Germanic *tiugī̆, *teug, from Proto-Germanic *teugą (“stuff, matter, device, gear, lever”, literally “that which is drawn or pulled”), from Proto-Germanic *teuhaną (“to lead, bring, pull”), from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to pull, lead”).

senses.d: Something to play with, especially as intended for use by a child.
ex: A grown man like him does not play with a child’s toy.

senses.d: A thing of little importance or value; a trifle.
ex: tis a pretie toy to be a Poet.

senses.d: A simple, light piece of music, written especially for the virginal.
A vague fancy, a ridiculous idea or notion; a whim.
ex: To fly about playing their wanton toys.
What if a toy take 'em i'th' heels now, and they all run away.

senses.d: An old story; a silly tale.
ex: More strange than true: I never may believe these antique fables, nor these fairy toys.

senses.d: A headdress of linen or wool that hangs down over the shoulders, worn by elderly women of the lower classes.
ex: Having, moreover, put on her clean toy, rokelay, and scarlet plaid.
It is incorrect to say that toys tag and masters piece; toys just do bad tags, bad throw-ups, and bad pieces.
I was a toy until I met Sear, who moved here from Toronto and showed me the book Subway Art.

senses.d: To play (with) in an idle or desultory way.
ex: to toy with a piece of food on one’s plate
Figo is toying with the English defence.
I have been toying with the idea of starting my own business.

senses.d: To stimulate with a sex toy.
ex: He could see her hand go to her slit, and soon she was toying herself along, breathing heavily.

senses.d: Impractical or unsuitable for real-world use, due to being unrealistically small or simple.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French jouet, corresponding to jouer + -et.
From jugar + -ete. Cognate with rare English jokette.

it:giocare.gl: to play a game, for fun or as a pastime

ety.text: Inherited from Latin iocārī. By surface analysis, gioco (“game”) + -are. Cognate with Sicilian jucari.

pt:jogar.gl: to play (to participate in a sport or game)

ety.text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese jogar, from Latin iocārī. Compare Galician xogar, Asturian xugar, Spanish jugar.

it:giocherellare.gl: to play, to fumble, to fiddle
